title: Respiration in Plants
tagline: Glycolysis, the link reaction, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain.

overview.intro: Respiration is the controlled release of energy from food, and the plant syllabus follows it through four stages: glycolysis in the cytoplasm, the link reaction and Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix, and the electron transport chain on the inner membrane. This chapter traces the carbon path and the energy yield of each stage, distinguishes aerobic from anaerobic respiration with its two fermentation end products, compares respiration with photosynthesis, and shows how to read the respiratory quotient, which is the standard numerical question in this area.

learningOutcomes: Describe glycolysis with its inputs, outputs and energy gain.
Trace the link reaction and Krebs cycle and state where each occurs.
Explain oxidative phosphorylation and chemiosmosis in the mitochondrion.
Distinguish aerobic and anaerobic respiration and give fermentation equations.
Calculate the respiratory quotient and interpret what it indicates about the substrate.

blocks.text: Glycolysis is the universal first stage of respiration, occurring in the cytoplasm of every living cell and requiring no oxygen, so it is described as anaerobic even when the rest of the pathway later runs aerobically. The pathway splits one molecule of glucose, a six-carbon compound, into two molecules of pyruvate, a three-carbon compound, in ten enzymatic steps of which the first two are investment steps. Glucose is phosphorylated using ATP to glucose-6-phosphate, isomerised to fructose-6-phosphate and phosphorylated again to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, so the cell has spent two ATP to activate the sugar. The six-carbon compound is then split into two three-carbon molecules, one of which is rearranged so that both can proceed as glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate. In the payoff steps each glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate is oxidised to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate with the reduction of NAD+ to NADH, then converted to 3-phosphoglycerate while phosphorylating ADP to ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation; a second ATP is gained later in the pathway. Because everything happens twice for each glucose, the yield is four ATP formed against two invested, a net gain of two ATP, together with two NADH and two pyruvate. The importance of glycolysis lies partly in its being the stage anaerobic organisms have and partly in it supplying the entry point — pyruvate — to the aerobic stages in the mitochondria.

items: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and does not require oxygen.
Investment phase: two ATP are spent phosphorylating glucose to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate.
The six-carbon sugar splits into two three-carbon compounds.
Payoff phase: NAD is reduced to NADH and ATP is formed by substrate-level phosphorylation.
Net yield per glucose: 2 ATP, 2 NADH and 2 pyruvate.
Pyruvate is the link to the aerobic stages in the mitochondrion.
The pathway is the same in plants, animals and microorganisms.

items.note: Oxygen cannot arrive fast enough, so pyruvate is fermented to lactic acid and the pathway that keeps producing ATP is glycolysis alone.
Yeast ferments pyruvate to ethanol and carbon dioxide, which is where the alcohol and the bubbles in bread and beer come from.

learn.title: The link reaction, Krebs cycle and electron transport chain

blocks.text: Aerobic respiration continues in the mitochondrion, a double-membraned organelle whose inner membrane is folded into cristae to increase the surface available for the electron transport chain. The link reaction takes pyruvate from the cytoplasm into the matrix, where it is decarboxylated to a two-carbon acetyl group and then combined with coenzyme A to form acetyl coenzyme A; one carbon dioxide is released and NAD+ is reduced to NADH for each pyruvate, so this step is the first point at which carbon leaves as carbon dioxide. The Krebs cycle, in the matrix, then oxidises the acetyl group completely: it combines with the four-carbon oxaloacetate to form citrate, and a series of reactions regenerates oxaloacetate while releasing two carbon dioxide and transferring energy to three NADH, one FADH2 and one ATP, or GTP, by substrate-level phosphorylation. Since each glucose gives two acetyl coenzyme A, the cycle turns twice per glucose, giving four carbon dioxide — two from the link reaction and four from the cycle in total, matching the six in the equation — and the products are six NADH, two FADH2 and two ATP. The electron transport chain on the inner membrane then collects the hydrogen carried by NADH and FADH2: the electrons pass down a series of carriers, and their energy is used to pump protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space, building a gradient across the inner membrane. The protons return through ATP synthase, and the energy of their flow drives ATP formation — chemiosmosis, the same mechanism as in chloroplasts but driven by electrons from food rather than from light. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor, combining with the electrons and protons to form water; without it the chain backs up, NADH cannot be reoxidised, and the Krebs cycle stops. The complete oxidation of one glucose therefore yields about 38 ATP: two from glycolysis, two from the Krebs cycle and about 34 from oxidative phosphorylation, the exact figure depending on the shuttle used to bring the cytoplasmic NADH electrons in.

items.note: It blocks the final carrier of the electron transport chain, so oxygen is never used, the gradient collapses and ATP production stops even though oxygen is present.

items.note: A flying insect needs ATP faster than glycolysis alone can supply it, so its muscle is packed with cristae-rich mitochondria.

learn.title: Anaerobic respiration and the respiratory quotient

blocks.text: When oxygen is short, cells must regenerate NAD+ some other way or glycolysis stops, and fermentation provides that way. In plant and yeast cells, pyruvate is first decarboxylated to acetaldehyde with the release of carbon dioxide, and acetaldehyde is then reduced to ethanol using the hydrogen from NADH, which returns NAD+ to the pathway; the overall equation for alcoholic fermentation is C6H12O6 → 2C2H5OH + 2CO2 with a yield of only the two ATP of glycolysis. In animal muscle, pyruvate is reduced directly to lactic acid, with no carbon dioxide released, and the equation is C6H12O6 → 2C3H6O3. Both routes are incomplete oxidations: most of the chemical energy remains locked in the ethanol or lactic acid, which is why a fermenting organism must consume far more glucose than an aerobic one for the same energy return. The respiratory quotient, or RQ, exploits this difference numerically. It is the volume of carbon dioxide evolved divided by the volume of oxygen taken in during respiration. For a carbohydrate the figure is exactly one, since six molecules of carbon dioxide are released for six of oxygen taken. For a fat the figure is less than one — about 0.7 for tripalmitin — because the fatty acid chains are highly reduced and require more oxygen to oxidise fully than the carbohydrate skeleton would, so extra oxygen is consumed without a matching carbon dioxide release. For organic acids such as malic or oxalic acid the figure exceeds one, since they are already oxidised and release carbon dioxide without consuming proportional oxygen. For a germinating seed respiring a fat the RQ below one is the diagnostic evidence that the stored oil is being used rather than starch, and measuring it in a respirometer is the standard experiment behind this topic.

items: Fermentation regenerates NAD+ so that glycolysis can continue without oxygen.
Alcoholic fermentation: pyruvate → acetaldehyde → ethanol, releasing carbon dioxide; plants and yeast.
Lactic acid fermentation: pyruvate → lactic acid, no carbon dioxide; animal muscle.
Both give only the two ATP of glycolysis, leaving most energy unused in the product.
RQ is carbon dioxide evolved divided by oxygen consumed.
RQ is 1 for carbohydrates, about 0.7 for fats, and above 1 for organic acids.
An RQ below 1 in a germinating seed shows fat rather than starch is being respired.

learn.title: Comparing the pathways and the energy balance

blocks.text: Once the stages are known separately, the examination asks you to set them against one another, and the comparison turns on three questions: where does each occur, what does each need, and what does each give. Glycolysis alone runs in the cytoplasm, needs no oxygen and yields two ATP and two pyruvate, which is why it is the one pathway every organism shares. The link reaction and the Krebs cycle run in the mitochondrial matrix, require no oxygen directly themselves but depend on the regeneration of NAD+ and FAD, and load the carriers that the electron transport chain will use. Oxidative phosphorylation runs on the inner membrane, requires oxygen as the final acceptor, and yields the great majority of the ATP — about thirty-four of the thirty-eight. Anaerobic respiration stops after glycolysis and fermentation, so the two ATP of glycolysis are all that is gained and the rest of the energy remains locked in the ethanol or lactic acid. The arithmetic explains everything practical that follows from the topic. A sprinting athlete runs on glycolysis and lactic acid fermentation because oxygen cannot arrive fast enough, so the yield per glucose is about nineteen times lower than aerobic respiration, which is why sustained effort depends on breathing rate and why the debt is repaid afterwards in extra oxygen. A germinating seed in a waterlogged soil cannot respire aerobically because oxygen is excluded, so it ferments, wastes much of its stored food and may die — which is why drainage matters. Yeast fermentation gives ethanol and carbon dioxide, the basis of brewing and of bread rising, while the same organism with oxygen present respires aerobically and multiplies far faster. The control question is equally consistent: the respiratory quotient of one for carbohydrate, about 0.7 for fat and above one for organic acids tells you which fuel is being burned, and the shift towards a quotient below one in a germinating seed tells you its oil store is in use.

items: Glycolysis: cytoplasm, no oxygen, two ATP — shared by every living thing.

Electron transport chain: inner membrane, oxygen required, about thirty-four ATP.
Anaerobic routes stop at fermentation and give only the two ATP of glycolysis.
One glucose gives about thirty-eight ATP aerobically against two anaerobically.
Lactic acid in muscle explains oxygen debt and the ache after a sprint.
Waterlogging forces fermentation in roots and seeds because oxygen is excluded.
The respiratory quotient identifies the fuel: one for carbohydrate, about 0.7 for fat.

questions.explanation: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and requires no oxygen or organelle.

questions.prompt: The net gain of ATP from glycolysis of one glucose molecule is:
questions.explanation: Four ATP are formed during the payoff steps but two are invested in the preparation, leaving a net gain of two.

questions.prompt: The final electron acceptor in aerobic respiration is:
questions.explanation: Oxygen accepts electrons and protons at the end of the chain to form water.

questions.prompt: The respiratory quotient for a fat respiring is:
questions.explanation: Fats are highly reduced and need more oxygen than the carbon dioxide they release, giving an RQ near 0.7.

questions.prompt: The breakdown of glucose to pyruvate in the cytoplasm is called __________.
questions.explanation: The word means splitting of sugar and occurs in all living cells.

questions.prompt: The inner membrane of the mitochondrion is folded into structures called __________ to increase the surface area for the electron transport chain.
questions.explanation: Cells with high energy demand have mitochondria with many closely packed cristae.

questions.prompt: Write the equation for alcoholic fermentation and state where it occurs.
questions.answer: The equation is C6H12O6 → 2C2H5OH + 2CO2, showing that one glucose yields two molecules of ethanol, two molecules of carbon dioxide and a small amount of energy. It occurs in the cytoplasm of plant cells and yeast under anaerobic conditions, after glycolysis has produced pyruvate. Pyruvate is first decarboxylated to acetaldehyde, releasing carbon dioxide, and acetaldehyde is then reduced to ethanol using hydrogen from NADH, which regenerates NAD+ so that glycolysis can continue. Only the two ATP of glycolysis are gained, because most of the energy remains in the ethanol.
questions.explanation: Balanced equation, the two steps with the NAD+ regeneration, the location and the ATP yield.

questions.prompt: What is the respiratory quotient and what does a value below one indicate?
questions.answer: The respiratory quotient is the ratio of the volume of carbon dioxide evolved to the volume of oxygen taken in during respiration over a given period. A value of one indicates that a carbohydrate is being oxidised, because six molecules of carbon dioxide are released for every six of oxygen consumed. A value below one, typically about 0.7, indicates that a fat is being respired: the fatty acid chains are highly reduced, so they require more oxygen for complete oxidation than the carbon dioxide balance would give, and oxygen is consumed in excess of carbon dioxide released. In a germinating seed an RQ below one is the standard evidence that stored oil rather than starch is being used.
questions.explanation: Definition, the carbohydrate value of one, and the reason fats give a lower figure.

questions.prompt: Name the three stages of aerobic respiration after glycolysis and state where each occurs.
questions.answer: After glycolysis in the cytoplasm, pyruvate enters the mitochondrion for the link reaction in the matrix, where it is decarboxylated to acetyl coenzyme A with the release of carbon dioxide. The Krebs cycle then runs in the matrix, oxidising the acetyl group completely and loading NADH and FADH2 while releasing more carbon dioxide. The electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane uses the hydrogen carried by those carriers to build a proton gradient that drives ATP synthesis, with oxygen acting as the final acceptor and forming water.
questions.explanation: Link reaction and Krebs cycle in the matrix, electron transport chain on the inner membrane, with the product of each.

questions.prompt: Describe the Krebs cycle and account for the products of one turn of it.
questions.answer: The Krebs cycle takes place in the mitochondrial matrix and begins when the two-carbon acetyl group of acetyl coenzyme A, produced by the link reaction, condenses with the four-carbon compound oxaloacetate to form the six-carbon citrate. A series of reactions then rearranges and decarboxylates the molecule: two carbon atoms leave as carbon dioxide, and the remaining four-carbon skeleton is regenerated as oxaloacetate so that the cycle can accept the next acetyl group. Along the way energy is transferred to electron carriers rather than to ATP directly: three molecules of NAD+ are reduced to NADH and one molecule of FAD is reduced to FADH2, while one ATP — or equivalently GTP — is formed by substrate-level phosphorylation. Each turn therefore consumes one acetyl group, releases two carbon dioxide and produces three NADH, one FADH2 and one ATP. Since each glucose yields two acetyl coenzyme A through the link reaction, the cycle turns twice per glucose and the products double: four carbon dioxide from the cycle, together with two from the link reaction, account for all six carbons of the glucose, while the six NADH and two FADH2 pass their stored hydrogen to the electron transport chain where the great majority of the ATP will be made.
questions.explanation: The condensation with oxaloacetate, the decarboxylations and regeneration, the per-turn products with the ATP mechanism, and the doubling per glucose with the carbon accounting.

questions.prompt: Explain why anaerobic respiration yields far less energy than aerobic respiration even though it starts from the same glucose.
questions.answer: The difference lies in how completely the glucose is oxidised. In anaerobic respiration the pathway stops at the products of fermentation — ethanol and carbon dioxide, or lactic acid — and these are still highly reduced compounds in which much of the chemical energy of the original glucose remains stored in their carbon-hydrogen bonds. The cell captures only the two ATP formed during glycolysis, because without oxygen the electron transport chain cannot operate, NADH cannot be reoxidised through it, and the Krebs cycle soon halts for want of NAD+. Aerobic respiration, by contrast, carries the oxidation all the way to carbon dioxide and water, which are the fully oxidised end products in which almost no usable energy remains. The link reaction and the Krebs cycle strip the hydrogen from the intermediates into NADH and FADH2, and the electron transport chain uses the energy of those electrons to pump protons and drive the synthesis of some 34 ATP, so about 38 molecules are obtained from one glucose rather than two — roughly nineteen times as much. The energy is released in small controlled steps rather than as one burst of heat, which is what makes aerobic respiration both more efficient and safer for the cell.
questions.explanation: Complete versus incomplete oxidation, what blocks the aerobic stages without oxygen, the ATP figures, and the controlled stepwise release.

questions.prompt: A student measures gas exchange in a germinating seed and finds the volume of carbon dioxide released equals the volume of oxygen absorbed. Predict the food store being used and state what would change if the seedlings grew green leaves and began photosynthesising in light.
questions.answer: A respiratory quotient of exactly one means the volume of carbon dioxide evolved equals the volume of oxygen absorbed, which is the ratio for a carbohydrate: six molecules of carbon dioxide are released for every six of oxygen consumed in the complete oxidation of glucose. The seed is therefore respiring a carbohydrate store such as starch rather than an oil, since a fat would give a quotient near 0.7, with extra oxygen consumed to oxidise the reduced fatty acid chains. If the seedlings developed green leaves and were given light, photosynthesis would begin, and the gas exchange measured would then be a balance of two processes rather than respiration alone: photosynthesis consumes carbon dioxide and releases oxygen, so while the light is bright enough the net carbon dioxide output would fall, may become zero, and could reverse to a net uptake, driving the apparent quotient towards zero or making it meaningless as a measure of respiration. To measure respiration in such a seedling the experiment would have to be run in darkness, where only respiration proceeds.
questions.explanation: Interpretation of RQ 1 as carbohydrate, the contrast with fat, then the effect of photosynthesis on gas exchange and the dark control.
